slides: Open by treating circle inversion as the chapter's engine rather than as an isolated trick. The rule looks simple, but it changes lines into circles, organizes coaxal pencils, explains ratio loci, and prepares the three-dimensional and elliptic-plane viewpoints at the end.

Use the route slide to name the transformations before the audience sees many circles at once. The sequence is radial inversion, image classification, orthogonal pencils, Apollonius loci, Mobius circle preservation, sphere inversion with stereographic projection, and finally great-circle intuition for the elliptic plane.

For inversion, keep the product law in the foreground. Each point travels along its ray from the center until the product of its old and new distances is the radius squared. The notebook checks both the product residual and the involution residual at machine precision.

The line and circle slide is the practical classification theorem. Lines through the inversion center remain lines, lines missing the center become circles through it, circles through the center become lines, and circles missing the center remain circles. The residuals certify all four cases numerically.

Orthogonal and coaxal pencils provide the structural view of circle families. The figure shows one pencil sharing limiting data and another family cutting it at right angles. The near-zero cosine check is the visible statement that orthogonality survives the construction.

Apollonius loci translate a distance ratio into a geometric object. When the ratio is one the locus is a line, and otherwise it is a circle whose center and radius move with the ratio. The table makes the transition around one inspectable rather than mysterious.

A Mobius transformation is the analytic version of circle preservation. The map may send a line to a circle or a circle to another generalized circle, but the cross-ratio remains stable. The fitted residuals show the sampled images really are generalized circles.

The sphere slide lifts the same inversion logic into three dimensions and pairs it with stereographic projection. Points remain collinear with the projection center along rays, the product law still holds, and the sphere equation residual confirms the sampled points stay on the intended sphere.

Elliptic-plane intuition asks students to reinterpret straightness. Antipodal points are identified, and great circles play the role of lines. The gnomonic triangle gives a concrete angle sum exceeding pi, with the spherical excess matching the solid angle area.

Close by connecting the artifacts as one transformation story. Inversion supplies the radial rule, line and circle images provide the classification, coaxal pencils and Apollonius loci organize families, Mobius maps preserve generalized circles, and sphere or elliptic models extend the same ideas upward.
